questions: How do false content, intent, selection, and biased transmission differ in the assessment of misleading communication?

used_for: True information can produce a false impression

evidence.excerpt: Another paradigm, widely used by philosophers to explore social aspects of epistemology, are epistemic network models.

For this reason, philosophers of science have tended to use the network epistemology framework introduced by economists Bala and Goyal (1998) to model how more rational individuals learn from neighbors.
As this model progresses these agents gather data, which increases their neighbors’ degrees of belief in turn.
In tightly connected networks, misleading evidence is widely shared, and may cause the community to pre-emptively settle on a poor theory.
This supports central claims from social epistemology espoused by Goldman (1999).
This can lead to stable, polarized camps that each ignore evidence and testimony coming from the other camp.
Other literature investigates the role of pernicious influencers, especially from industry, on epistemic communities.
One truth about epistemic communities is that relationships matter.
The latest challenge confronting the informational state of the public is the accelerating spread of misleading content on the internet.
Others have challenged the idea that disinformation needs to be misleading, as opposed to producing ignorance (Simion 2023) or otherwise blocking successful action (Harris 2023).
Lynch (2018) argues that epistemic arrogance, which involves an unwillingness to learn from others, undermines the process of public debate.
There have been concerns that various aspects of this process may exacerbate false beliefs.
This is sometimes called the “filter bubble” or “information bubble” effect (though these various phenomena are by no means clearly delineated) (Pariser 2011, Kitchens et al. 2020).
This includes understanding social aspects of knowledge and belief formation.
